result: At the neuroma site following nerve injury, Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 expression (normally localized to the juxtaparanode) is markedly decreased at days 7 and 21 post-injury, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis.
evaluation: Claims C3, C43, C70, and C73 provide converging evidence from both immunohistochemistry (showing reduced percentage of Kv1.2-positive nodes from 86.1% to 8.3%) and Western blot analysis (showing significant reduction at days 7 and 21) at the neuroma site. The data are quantified with appropriate statistics (n=4 animals, p<0.001) and supported by Figure 1.

result: Following nerve injury in rats, Kv1.4 and Kv1.6, which are barely detectable in naive axons (Kv1.4: 5.5±4.6% of nodes; Kv1.6: absent), show significantly increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes at the neuroma site by day 21 (Kv1.4: 73.3±12%; Kv1.6: 66.6±14%).
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C44, C49, C50, C71, C72, and C74 collectively demonstrate a robust switch in Kv1 channel subunit composition. The data are supported by both immunohistochemistry (showing percentage of positive nodes) and Western blot analysis (showing significant upregulation) with appropriate sample sizes (n=4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal) and statistics (p<0.001). Figure 1 provides visual confirmation.

result: Similar to rats, human neuroma tissue shows decreased Kv1.2 expression (from 90±10% to 13.3±8.1% of nodes) and increased Kv1.4 (92.5±7.4%) and Kv1.6 (73.5±8.8%) expression following injury, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis.
evaluation: Claims C7, C81-C86 demonstrate that the Kv1 channel subunit switch observed in rats is conserved in human pathology. The data include both immunohistochemistry (n=3 per group, 8-10 nodes per patient) and Western blot analysis (n=6 per group) with appropriate statistics (Mann-Whitney U-Test, p=0.005). Figure 7 provides supporting evidence. The translational relevance strengthens the findings.

result: At day 7 after injury at the neuroma site, Kv1.2 channels and caspr2 redistribute from the juxtaparanode to overlap with paranodal proteins (caspr), moving closer to the node, as demonstrated by quantitative distance measurements showing negative overlap values.
evaluation: Claims C52, C54, C55, C56, and C58 provide quantitative evidence of Kv1 channel redistribution. The distance measurements show that while Nav-caspr distance remains unchanged (4±0.1 μm), the Nav-Kv1.2 distance decreases significantly (3.2±0.2 μm), resulting in negative overlap (-0.8±0.1 μm, n=3 animals, 32-35 nodes per animal). Similar data for caspr2 (-1.2±0.1 μm) support coordinated movement of the Kv1 channel complex. Figure 3 provides visual confirmation.

result: The redistribution of Kv1.2 and caspr2 toward the paranode occurs not only at the neuroma site but also at sites proximal to the injury (1 cm away), indicating a widespread axonal response rather than a purely local effect.
evaluation: Claims C59 and C60 demonstrate that Kv1 channel redistribution is not confined to the injury site. Quantitative measurements show similar Kv1.2 redistribution at both sites (neuroma: -1±0.09 μm; proximal: -1.1±0.09 μm, p=0.6), while caspr2 redistribution is slightly less pronounced but still significant at the proximal site (-0.5±0.1 μm vs -1±0.1 μm, p=0.06, both significantly different from naive p<0.001). Sample size is adequate (n=5 animals, 21-26 nodes per animal).

result: Electron microscopy analysis reveals that paranodal ultrastructure is largely preserved after injury, with no major disruption of septate axoglial junctions, though there is a small but significant increase in maximal distance between paranodal loops (from 12.5±1 nm to 18.9±1.4 nm, p=0.005).
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 provide ultrastructural evidence that paranodal junction integrity is maintained. The axo-glial distance remains unchanged (9.7±0.4 nm vs 11.4±0.7 nm, p=0.08), and axonal diameter at the node is stable. The small increase in maximal interloop distance is statistically significant but modest. Sample size is adequate (n=4-5 animals, 6-9 nodes per animal). Figure 4 provides visual confirmation. This suggests that Kv1 redistribution is not due to gross structural disruption.

result: βII spectrin, a cytoskeletal protein that acts as a barrier to lateral diffusion of Kv1 channels, shows reduced expression at the paranodal domain (to 0.4±0.02 of naive, p<0.001) and in the DRG (to 0.7±0.08, p=0.04) following nerve injury, which is compatible with the observed lateral movement of Kv1 channels into the paranode.
evaluation: Claims C65-C69, C130, and C131 provide a mechanistic explanation for Kv1 channel redistribution. The reduction in βII spectrin is demonstrated by both immunohistochemistry (n=50-83 heminodes) and Western blot (n=4) with appropriate statistics. The inference that reduced βII spectrin allows lateral diffusion of Kv1 channels (C131) is reasonable given established knowledge (C65-C66) and is supported by prior literature showing similar effects in βII spectrin knockout mice. Figure 5 provides supporting data.

result: In the DRG, Kv1.2 expression is significantly reduced following nerve injury, while Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 expression remains unchanged, suggesting that increased axonal expression of Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 at the neuroma results from altered trafficking rather than global upregulation.
evaluation: Claims C75-C80 distinguish between somatic and axonal changes in Kv1 channel expression. The data show reduced Kv1.2 in DRG (consistent with prior literature, C77) but stable Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 (C79), while axonal expression of Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 increases. The inference about altered trafficking (C80) is logical and supported by the data. Sample size is adequate (n=6 per group, one-way ANOVA). Figure 6 provides supporting evidence.

result: In the dorsal root (remote from the injury site), Kv1 channels gradually redistribute to the paranode by day 21 post-injury, with Kv1.2 showing significant overlap with caspr (-1.4±0.3 μm, p<0.001), and novel expression of Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 appearing in both juxtaparanodal and paranodal regions.
evaluation: Claims C8, C45, C87-C92 demonstrate that Kv1 channel redistribution occurs at sites distant from the injury. The temporal progression is documented (no overlap at day 7, significant overlap by day 21), and quantitative measurements are provided for all three Kv1 subunits. Caspr2 also redistributes similarly (C92). Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-5 animals, 25-40 nodes per animal). Figure 8 provides visual confirmation. This indicates a coordinated axonal response to injury.

result: Spontaneous activity in myelinated afferents increases acutely after nerve injury (to 22% at day 2) then decreases over time (to 6.2% at day 7 and 2.5% at day 21). Application of α-DTX (Kv1 channel blocker) has no effect in naive axons but significantly reinstates spontaneous activity at days 7 and 21 post-injury, indicating that Kv1 channels play a role in recovery from hyperexcitability.
evaluation: Claims C93-C100 provide electrophysiological evidence for the functional role of Kv1 channels. The temporal pattern of spontaneous activity is well-documented with adequate sample sizes (n=4-10 animals, 222-291 neurons per condition). The effect of α-DTX is statistically significant at later timepoints (day 7: 15.6% with DRG toxin, p=0.002; day 21: 17.7% with DRG toxin, p<0.001) but not at baseline or day 2. Chi-square tests are appropriate for proportion data. Figure 9 provides supporting traces. The inference about Kv1 channel role (C100) is well-supported.

result: At day 21 post-injury, α-DTX application significantly increases the proportion of neurons responding to mechanical stimulation with a 15g von Frey filament (from 24.7% to 30.5%, p=0.006), demonstrating that Kv1 channels suppress mechanosensitivity of afferents innervating the neuroma.
evaluation: Claims C101 and C147 demonstrate that Kv1 channels modulate mechanical sensitivity. The effect is statistically significant with adequate sample size (n=259 neurons). Chi-square test is appropriate for proportion data. The effect is specific to the 15g stimulus, with trends at lower forces. Figure 9 provides supporting traces. This complements the spontaneous activity data.

result: Behavioral testing shows that mechanical withdrawal thresholds decrease acutely after injury (to 8.2±0.6g at day 3) then gradually recover (to 44.8±1.6g at day 21). α-DTX injection prevents this recovery, maintaining low thresholds at days 7 (6.9±0.9g, p=0.003) and 21 (13±2.1g, p<0.001), demonstrating that Kv1 channels are responsible for the partial recovery of mechanical hypersensitivity.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 and C148 provide behavioral evidence supporting the electrophysiological findings. The temporal pattern of recovery is well-documented, and the effect of α-DTX is statistically significant at both day 7 and day 21. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-9 animals per group), and repeated measures two-way ANOVA is appropriate for the experimental design. Figure 10 provides supporting data. The conclusion that Kv1 channels mediate recovery is well-supported by the convergent electrophysiological and behavioral evidence.

result: The effects of α-DTX on mechanical hypersensitivity are likely mediated through Kv1.6 rather than Kv1.4, as CP 339818 hydrochloride (a selective Kv1.3/Kv1.4 blocker) has no effect on mechanical hypersensitivity at any timepoint, while α-DTX (which blocks Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.6) is effective when Kv1.6 expression is increased.
evaluation: Claims C106-C109 and C150 provide pharmacological evidence for the specific role of Kv1.6. The negative result with CP 339818 (n=7-8 animals, p>0.05) combined with the positive effect of α-DTX and the expression pattern (Kv1.1/1.2 decreased, Kv1.6 increased) support the inference that Kv1.6 is the key mediator. However, the inference (C150) acknowledges uncertainty ('most probably') which is appropriate given that α-DTX also blocks Kv1.1 and Kv1.2, and channels likely form heteromultimers.

result: The main conclusion of the study is that changes in the molecular composition (increased Kv1.4 and Kv1.6, decreased Kv1.1 and Kv1.2) and distribution (redistribution to paranodes) of axonal Kv1 channels represent a protective mechanism to suppress hyperexcitability of myelinated sensory axons following nerve injury.
evaluation: Claims C11, C46, and C120 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from: (1) immunohistochemistry and Western blot showing altered Kv1 channel expression and distribution in both rats and humans; (2) electrophysiological recordings showing that Kv1 blockade reinstates hyperexcitability; (3) behavioral testing showing that Kv1 blockade prevents recovery from mechanical hypersensitivity; and (4) mechanistic data on βII spectrin reduction. The inference is logical and supported by the data.

result: In naive axons, over 90% of nodes show typical morphology with Nav at the center flanked by caspr and Kv1.2 in the juxtaparanode, but at the neuroma site (days 7 and 21), only about half of nodes maintain this typical morphology, with the remainder showing split, heminode, or naked configurations.
evaluation: Claims C47 and C51 document the disruption of nodal architecture at the injury site. The quantification is adequate (n=4 animals per group, 36-64 nodes per animal) and shows a clear difference between naive (91±2.9% typical) and injured (47.5±5.1% at day 7, 46±6% at day 21) conditions. This provides important context for interpreting the Kv1 channel redistribution data. Figure 2 provides visual examples of the different node types.
